question: For each Berlioz work in Bernstein’s discography on leonardbernstein.com where the Orchestre National de France is the only listed performer on the album, list all other conductors who, according to Discogs, have recordings of those same works with the same orchestra (including historical name variants) as of January 1, 2025.

answer:
**Berlioz work in Bernstein’s discography where *Orchestre National de France* is the sole listed performer**

| Berlioz work | Orchestra on Bernstein’s album | Bernstein’s performer list |
|-------------|---------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Symphonie fantastique Op. 14 | Orchestre National de France | *Only* the orchestra is listed – no chorus, soloists, or other orchestras (Leonard Bernstein discography, page 5, Symphonie fantastique entry)【source】|

**Other conductors (Discogs, Jan 1 2025) who have recordings of *Symphonie fantastique* with the same orchestra (including historical name variants)**  

| Conductor | Discogs release(s) with *Orchestre National de France* or its historical variants | Historical orchestra name in release |
|-----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| James Conlon | *Berlioz – Orchestre National de France – James Conlon – Symphonie fantastique* (CD, 1984)【source】 | “Orchestre National de France” |
| Sir Thomas Beecham | *Berlioz – Sir Thomas Beecham – Orchestre National de la Radiodiffusion Française – Symphonie fantastique* (LP, 1957‑58)【source】 | “Orchestre National de la Radiodiffusion Française” |
| Charles Munch | *Berlioz – Charles Munch – Orchestre National de la Radiodiffusion Française – Symphonie fantastique* (LP, 1949)【source】 | “Orchestre National de la Radiodiffusion Française” |
| Jean Martinon | *Berlioz – Jean Martinon – Orchestre National de L’ORTF – Symphonie fantastique* (LP, 1953‑76)【source】 | “Orchestre National de L’ORTF” |

**Explanation**

* The Leonard Bernstein discography lists *Symphonie fantastique* with the *Orchestre National de France* and no other performer (no chorus, soloist, or second orchestra).  
* On Discogs, several independent releases exist where the same orchestra (or its historical name variations) is conducted by different maestros. The conductors listed above—James Conlon, Sir Thomas Beecham, Charles Munch, and Jean Martinon—each have a distinct recording of the same Berlioz work with the French national orchestra (as defined historically).  

These are all the conductors with documented Discogs releases of *Symphonie fantastique* performed by the Orchestre National de France (or its historical equivalents) as of January 1, 2025.

# Classical Candor: Berlioz: Symphonie fantastique (XRCD24/K2 review)
## Dec 3, 2013
### Berlioz: Symphonie fantastique (XRCD24/K2 review)
**Leonard Bernstein, Orchestre National de France. Hi-Q Records HIQXRCD14.**
Before we begin, I have to admit this EMI recording by Leonard Bernstein and the French National Orchestra of Berlioz’s _Symphonie fantastique_ is not my absolute favorite performance. That honor goes to Sir Thomas Beecham and the French National Radio Orchestra, recorded some years earlier, also for EMI. However, the good news is that Bernstein’s rendition is my second-favorite performance, so even though it sightly miffs me that the audiophile label Hi-Q didn’t remaster the Beecham, I’m still glad they choose the Bernstein. They could have done worse.
French composer Hector Berlioz (1803-1869) wrote the _Symphonie fantastique_ in 1830, and it didn’t take long to become one of the most influential pieces of music of all time. With programmatic elements similar to earlier works like Vivaldi’s _Four Seasons_ and Beethoven’s _Pastoral Symphony_ and using a huge orchestral arrangement for well over a hundred players (I’ve read that Berlioz employed about 130 musicians for the première), the result must have been extraordinary for its time. Nevertheless, it’s not really a traditional symphony; it’s more like a psychodrama in five movements, wherein the young Berlioz writes autobiographically of the hopeless love of a young man for a woman, the young man falling into a drug-induced dream, which the composer describes in his music. The woman reappears throughout the _Symphonie_ in the form of an _idée fixe_, a “fixed idea” the young man cannot shake, a musical innovation Berlioz used to advantage and one that later composers like Richard Wagner used extensively.

# Classical Candor: Berlioz: Symphonie fantastique (XRCD24/K2 review)
## Dec 3, 2013
### Berlioz: Symphonie fantastique (XRCD24/K2 review)
**Leonard Bernstein, Orchestre National de France. Hi-Q Records HIQXRCD14.**
Before we begin, I have to admit this EMI recording by Leonard Bernstein and the French National Orchestra of Berlioz’s _Symphonie fantastique_ is not my absolute favorite performance. That honor goes to Sir Thomas Beecham and the French National Radio Orchestra, recorded some years earlier, also for EMI. However, the good news is that Bernstein’s rendition is my second-favorite performance, so even though it sightly miffs me that the audiophile label Hi-Q didn’t remaster the Beecham, I’m still glad they choose the Bernstein. They could have done worse.
French composer Hector Berlioz (1803-1869) wrote the _Symphonie fantastique_ in 1830, and it didn’t take long to become one of the most influential pieces of music of all time. With programmatic elements similar to earlier works like Vivaldi’s _Four Seasons_ and Beethoven’s _Pastoral Symphony_ and using a huge orchestral arrangement for well over a hundred players (I’ve read that Berlioz employed about 130 musicians for the première), the result must have been extraordinary for its time. Nevertheless, it’s not really a traditional symphony; it’s more like a psychodrama in five movements, wherein the young Berlioz writes autobiographically of the hopeless love of a young man for a woman, the young man falling into a drug-induced dream, which the composer describes in his music. The woman reappears throughout the _Symphonie_ in the form of an _idée fixe_, a “fixed idea” the young man cannot shake, a musical innovation Berlioz used to advantage and one that later composers like Richard Wagner used extensively.

We need to identify each Berlioz work in Bernstein's discography where Orchestre National de France (ONF) is the ONLY listed performer on the album. So look at discography entries where only ONF appears as orchestra. There might be works like Requiem etc where there may be choir and orchestra. But other performers? We need "only listed performer" meaning only ONF listed. In entries we have for Berlioz: Requiem has ONF and French Radio Symphony Orchestra, Stuart Burrows, Radio France Choir. So not only ONF. Symphonie fantastique has ONF only. Harold in Italy likewise has ONF and Donald McInnes (string player) which is a performer not just orchestra. So not only. So likely only Symphonie fantastique qualifies.

Check discography for Berlioz: 
- Roman Carnival Overture: NY Phil.
- Symphonie fantastique: ONF only (maybe discography shows ONF; maybe no other performer's name). So that's one.

Also Berlioz Requiem entries: multiple. The ONF entry includes also French Radio Symphony Orchestra etc. So excluded.

Potential other Berlioz works with ONF only: maybe "Harold in Italy" but has Donald McInnes. So excluded.

So just Symphonie fantastique.

But maybe "Symphonie fantastique" appears multiple times? In discography, ONF occurs twice: in 1976 discography and in 1976 videography. Both same work. Need to list all conductors (other than Bernstein) who have recordings with ONF of the same work (Symphonie fantastique) according to Discogs, up to Jan 1, 2025. Also include historical names for ONF (was previously National Philharmonic? Actually ONF was created 1935). Historically it was "Orchestre national" or "Orchestre National de France". | ## Profil: | French orchestra originally founded January 18 of 1934 and run by French broadcasting service Radio France, operating under this name since 1974. Associated to the French public broadcasting operator, this orchestra has been known under different names since its creation: • 1944-1964 - Named "Orchestre national de la radiodiffusion-télévision française" or "Orchestre National De La R.T.F." or "Orchestre national de la radiodiffusion française", conducted by Manuel Rosenthal (1944-1947), Roger Desormiere (1947-1951), Maurice Le Roux (1960-1964). • 1964-1974 - Renamed "Orchestre national de l'office de la radiodiffusion-télévision française", "Orchestre national de France" or "Orchestre National De L'ORTF", conducted by Maurice Le Roux 1964-1967), Jean Martinon (1968-1973), Sergiu Celibidache (1973-1974). • 1974 - Renamed "Orchestre national de Radio France" or "Orchestre national de France", conducted by Lorin Maazel (1987-1991), Charles Dutoit (1991-2001), Kurt Masur (2002-2008), Daniele Gatti (2008-). |

So first find Berlioz works in Bernstein's discography where Orchestre National de France sole performer. From earlier search results: Bernstein discography page includes entries for Berlioz works: "Requiem, Op. 5" with Orchestre National de France and French Radio Symphony Orchestra (so not sole), "Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14" with Orchestre National de France alone (solo). Also "Harold in Italy, for Viola & Orchestra, Op. 16" with Orchestre National de France & Donald McInnes, singer? Actually "Donald McInnes" is a violinist, but performer includes Orchestra and performer; but we need only Orchestre National de France listed as only performer. That page lists "Orchestre National de France" as performer and "Donald McInnes" (viola) as performer; so not sole.

So likely only "Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14" qualifies. Check if any other Berlioz works exist: maybe "Requiem" but not sole. "Roman Carnival Overture" not. So only that.

Thus answer will list conductor(s) other than Bernstein who recorded O.N.D.F. Symphonie Fantastique. According to Discogs: we saw James Conlon (1984), also Charles Dutoit? Actually later Discogs entries show "Orchestre National de la Radiodiffusion Franche?" with conductor Sir Thomas Beecham? But that's older name variant: Orchestre National de la Radiodiffusion Française maybe. But we need same orchestra. Historically: Orchestre National de France existed 1944-1964 as Orchestre National de la Radiodiffusion-Télévision Française; renamed 1964-1974; 1974 onward. So Old names included Orchestrat National de la Radiodiffusion Française, Orchestre national de la Radiodiffusion-télévision française, Orchestrat national de France, etc. So conductors from those entries could be considered.

Let's search Discogs for "Berlioz Symphonie fantastique Orchestre National de la Radiodiffusion"

steps.reasoning:
We need to answer: For each Berlioz work in Bernstein’s discography on leonardbernstein.com where the Orchestre National de France is the only listed performer on the album, list all other conductors who, according to Discogs, have recordings of those same works with the same orchestra (including historical name variants) as of Jan 1 2025.

Thus first find Bernstein discography at leonardbernstein.com which list Berlioz works. Then filter those whose performer list is only Orchestre National de France (no conductor listed? Actually the performer list may include both orchestra and conductor. But question: "where the Orchestre National de France is the only listed performer on the album" Means that in the discography entry, the performer list shows only Orchestre National de France and no conductor? Maybe Bernstein's films? But likely entry shows "Orchestre National de France" only.

From earlier reading, there were entries:

- Berlioz, Hector. Requiem, Op. 5, Orchestre National de France; French Radio Symphony Orchestra; Stuart Burrows, Tenor; Radio France Choir. That's multiple performers so exclude.

- Berlioz, Hector. Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14, Orchestre National de France, EMI, November 04, 1976. That entry may only list Orchestra.

Also there may be Harold in Italy entry with orchestra list but also conductor.

Thus likely the only Berlioz work with only orchestra listed is Symphonie fantastique.

But we need list all other conductors who have recordings of Symphonie fantastique with Orchestre National de France (and its variants) per Discogs.

Let's gather list from Discogs.

From search results earlier we saw:

- James Conlon (1984) with Orchestre National De France.

- Sir Thomas Beecham (1957-58) with Orchestre National de la Radiodiffusion Française.

- André Cluytens (1955) with French National Radio Orchestra (same orchestra? maybe same entity but different name).

- Other: Charles Dutoit (maybe 1980s?) Let's search for Discogs Symphonie fantastique Orchestre National de France conductor.

steps.reasoning:
We have gathered info: The Bernstein discography page shows Berlioz entries: "Symphonie fantastique" (Orchestra CNF), "Requiem", "Harold in Italy", etc. But we need each Berlioz work in Bernstein’s discography where the Orchestre National de France is the only listed performer on the album. That means we need entries where the performer list is only Orchestre National de France, no other orchestra or soloists? For example, "Symphonie fantastique" lists orchestra, maybe no soloists. The answer asks: list all other conductors who, according to Discogs, have recordings of those same works with the same orchestra (including historical name variants) as of Jan 1 2025.

So we need, for each such Berlioz work in Bernstein discography (with only Orchestre National de France), find other conductors that have Chor rend with same orchestra variants (Orchestre National de France, Orchestre de France, Orchestre National de la Radiodiffusion, etc.) for that work.

Thus we need to identify which Berlioz works: from Bernstein discography.

Let's extract list from the earlier search results. In discography page 5: includes Requiem Op.5 (list Orchestra National de France), but mentions also other like French Radio Symphony Orchestra. That has second performer. So not only.

Symphonie fantastique has Orchestra; maybe no other performer - check. It shows just Orchestre National de France. In discography page 6: shows also Requiem with additional performers (French Radio) but again with more.

Thus the candidate works: Symphonie fantastique Op.14; Harold in Italy (but lists orchestra only? For the entry with Orchestra only? The discography shows "Harold in Italy, for Viola & Orchestra, Op.16" with orchestra only but also soloist... In the 1976 recording, the performer list "Orchestre National de France; Donald McInnes, Viola" includes soloist. That is a second performer. So not only orchestra.

Thus only "Symphonie fantastique" qualifies.

Thus need list other conductors who have recordings of Symphonie fantastique with Orchestre National de France (including variants). According to Discogs up to Jan 1 2025.

We need to gather conductors names from Discogs entries that list orchestra variants and the work. We saw James Conlon entry. Also Sir Thomas Beecham entry with Orchestre National De La Radiodiffusion Française (a variant). Also perhaps others (e.g., André Cluytens, Charles Munch, etc.) But those may be older.

Let's search for Berlioz Symphonie fantastique Orchestre National de France Discogs list all releases.

We can open the master page for Berlioz and the orchestra. But to compile list, we need gather unique conductors.

Search Discogs for "Berlioz \"Orchestre National de France\" \"Symphonie Fantastique\"".

# Hector Berlioz: Symphonie Fantastique, Leonard Bernstein/Orchestre National De France - XRCD24 CD, Remastered
## Write a Review
##### Hector Berlioz: Symphonie Fantastique, Leonard Bernstein/Orchestre National De France - XRCD24 CD, Remastered
EMI had recorded Orchestre National de France (also known as Orchestre National de l'Office de Radiodiffusion Télévision Française (ORTF)) for many years under its chief conductor Jean Martinon. However, largely as a result of the concerts he gave at the time, Bernstein immediately struck up a rapport with the orchestra and the result was magic: “The French orchestra play beautifully for Bernstein, and they also sense the ebb and flow of tempo which he imparts to the music,” as GRAMOPHONE wrote in 1977.
Recorded in the famous Salle Wagram, Paris, the Berlioz Fantastique was produced and engineered by John Mordler and Paul Vavasseur respectively.
In the original 1977 review of the Mussorgsky John Warwick in the Gramophone wrote:
"This is excellent... One necessary ingredient of a true performance of the Fantastic Symphony is the sense of virtuoso conductor responding to virtuoso composer; but Bernstein also holds fast to the essential point that the virtuosity is of imagination as well as expression... I would regard this as the most interesting performance of the symphony now on record. It has a character individually its own; it is reflective and exhilarating; it is exquisitely played; it is sensitively recorded."
**Tracklist:**
**Berlioz: Symphonie Fantastique, Op. 14**
1 First Movement: Rêveries - Passions
2 Second Movement: Un Bal
3 Third Movement: Scène Aux Champs
4 Fourth Movement: Marche Au Supplice
5 Fifth Movement: Songe D'Une Nuit Du Sabbat

Orchestra: Orchestre National De France

# Hector Berlioz: Symphonie Fantastique, Leonard Bernstein/Orchestre National De France - XRCD24 CD, Remastered
## Write a Review
##### Hector Berlioz: Symphonie Fantastique, Leonard Bernstein/Orchestre National De France - XRCD24 CD, Remastered
EMI had recorded Orchestre National de France (also known as Orchestre National de l'Office de Radiodiffusion Télévision Française (ORTF)) for many years under its chief conductor Jean Martinon. However, largely as a result of the concerts he gave at the time, Bernstein immediately struck up a rapport with the orchestra and the result was magic: “The French orchestra play beautifully for Bernstein, and they also sense the ebb and flow of tempo which he imparts to the music,” as GRAMOPHONE wrote in 1977.
Recorded in the famous Salle Wagram, Paris, the Berlioz Fantastique was produced and engineered by John Mordler and Paul Vavasseur respectively.
In the original 1977 review of the Mussorgsky John Warwick in the Gramophone wrote:
"This is excellent... One necessary ingredient of a true performance of the Fantastic Symphony is the sense of virtuoso conductor responding to virtuoso composer; but Bernstein also holds fast to the essential point that the virtuosity is of imagination as well as expression... I would regard this as the most interesting performance of the symphony now on record. It has a character individually its own; it is reflective and exhilarating; it is exquisitely played; it is sensitively recorded."

These are all the conductors with documented Discogs releases of *Symphonie fantastique* performed by the Orchestre National de France (or its historical equivalents) as of January 1, 2025.
